reports.headline: Eastern canyons wait on the warm push as shelf water lags behind the calendar
reports.subhead: With no fresh SST imagery since June 3 and the analyst pipeline thin, the early-June bite hinges on whether the 70-fathom edge has crossed into the mid-60s.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest opener this morning is that the data is thinner than I'd like. The most recent SST package in the catalog is dated June 3, and there has been no fresh thermal imagery to confirm whether the warm tongue that was probing the Atlantis west wall earlier in the week has consolidated or pulled back east. Buoy-side, the analyst feed is quiet on the offshore stations, which means we're reasoning from the last good look and from what the boats running this week are seeing under their hulls. That last look had shelf water in the upper 50s to low 60s inside the 100-fathom line, with the first real break to mid-60s sitting out along the 500-fathom contour from Veatch east through Hydrographer. That is a normal early-June posture out here — it is not yet a yellowfin posture.

What that means for the eastern canyon beat is simple: this is still a bluefin and early-mahi window, not a wide-open tuna fishery. The fish that respond first to a 62-to-64-degree shelf are mid-range bluefin on the troll and on the jig, working bait pods along the 50-to-70-fathom shelf edge rather than the canyon heads themselves. Veatch and the western edge of Atlantis are the percentage plays from Montauk and Block Island ports because the run is shorter and the bait line tends to set up there first as the warm water pivots in from the southwest. Oceanographer and the far eastern end stay a Rhode Island and south-of-the-Vineyard game until the surface temperatures climb another two or three degrees.

The on-the-water intelligence this week has been consistent with that read. Bluefin in the 50-to-80-inch class have been the dominant catch for boats willing to slow down and work bait marks rather than commit to a full canyon troll spread. Sand eels are still the controlling forage on the shelf, and that is keeping fish deep and keeping the jig bite — flutter jigs and heavy slow-pitch in 40 to 60 fathoms — more productive than the surface program. A handful of early mahi have shown on high-flyers and lobster gear out along the 100-fathom line, which is the first real signal that the warm water is fingering in, but the numbers are not there yet to justify a dedicated mahi run.

The yellowfin reports remain south and west — Hudson, Toms, the Lindenkohl complex — and that geography matches the temperature gradient. Until the 68-degree isotherm crosses the eastern canyon heads, the yellowfin will stay on the mid-Atlantic side of the picture. Bigeye are a night-troll lottery ticket at this stage of the season, worth a pull on the deep edges of Atlantis if you are already committed to an overnight, but not a target. White marlin and wahoo are still two to three weeks out under any reasonable read of the thermal progression.

Looking ahead three to five days, the pivot point is whether we get a sustained southwest flow to push the warm water up over the shelf break. A persistent southwesterly for 48 hours will move the 68-degree line measurably north and east, and that is the trigger I want to see before committing fuel to a full canyon overnight. The new moon falls into the window as well, which historically firms up the chunk and night-swordfish programs once the water cooperates. Without fresh SST in hand I am running the next trip as a bluefin trip with canyon options, not the other way around — meaning gear rigged for jigging and bait on the shelf edge, with a trolling spread ready to deploy if we mark a clean temperature break on the run out.

The eastern canyons are doing exactly what they do in the first week of June — teasing, not delivering. The boats catching fish right now are the ones reading bait and bottom rather than chasing a calendar. When the warm water arrives, it will arrive quickly, and Veatch will be the first to tell us.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Southern canyons wait on fresh thermal imagery as June troll window opens
reports.subhead: With SST products stalled at June 3 and no live buoy feed in hand, canyon strategy hinges on the last known edge positions and the calendar.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest truth about the south canyon grounds this morning is that the picture is partially obscured. The most recent SST package in the catalog is dated June 3, and there has been no June 4 or June 5 imagery pushed through the pipeline yet. Offshore buoy readings did not make it into today's analyst brief either, so anything I tell you about the Spencer-to-Norfolk corridor has to be reasoned from the last clean look at the water rather than a fresh snapshot. That last look, from the May 31 through June 3 sequence, had the warm side of the shelf-slope front sitting in the high 60s to around 70 on the inshore lip of Spencer and Lindenkohl, with the blue water pushing up into the notches as the Gulf Stream meander to the south kept feeding warm filaments north and west. Sea state and wind are not in today's data set, so anyone running tomorrow needs to pull their own NDBC 44009 and 44025 readings before they untie.

What that means for the beat is straightforward. June 5 is right in the front edge of the yellowfin troll window for the southern canyons, and the fish that show up first almost always set up on the 100-fathom curve where the temperature break stacks against structure — the east wall of Spencer, the southwest corner of Lindenkohl, and the deeper fingers off Poor Man's. With the last imagery showing the warm push leaning into the canyon heads rather than washing over the top, I would be running to the 500-fathom line first, working the temperature gradient back inshore until the trolling spread tells you where the bait column is sitting. Bigeye are a dawn-and-dusk proposition this early, and the water has not been warm enough long enough to expect a real wahoo or mahi pick on the high-flyers and lobster pots yet, though a stray gaffer dolphin around any floating debris is not out of the question.

The pattern that was developing through the end of May had the cleanest blue water and the most consistent life pinned to Lindenkohl and the stretch between Lindenkohl and Spencer. Norfolk, further south and east out of Ocean City, was showing the more aggressive thermal contrast on the June 2 and June 3 charts — a tighter break, more chlorophyll edge — but it is a longer run and you want a confirmed report or fresh imagery before you commit to that fuel burn. Poor Man's has been the swing canyon, sometimes lighting up when the closer grounds are flat, and it deserves a look on the way home if you have the daylight.

Looking ahead three to five days, the variables I am watching are the return of SST imagery — once the June 4 and June 5 composites land, the edge positions will either confirm that warm push is holding into the canyon heads or show it has slid back off to the southeast, which would push the bite further offshore and reset the run. The other piece is the moon. We are working away from the full and into the last quarter through the back half of the week, which historically lines up with the first real chunking windows on overnight trips once water hits the low 70s consistently. If the next imagery cycle shows 70-plus on the inshore side of the break at Spencer or Lindenkohl, that is the trigger to start planning overnighters rather than day-troll missions.

I'd treat the next 48 hours as reconnaissance. Run the troll, mark your temperature breaks by hand, log bait shows and any life on the surface, and bring that intel back so the next trip can be fished on real information rather than a three-day-old chart. The canyons are opening up. The data just has not caught up to the calendar yet.

reports.headline: Washington Canyon opens June with stale SST data but a textbook early-season setup
reports.subhead: Latest published thermal imagery is two days stale, but the Gulf Stream's western wall position still favors the south side troll.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk is running thin this morning. The most recent published SST package in the catalog is dated June 3, and the analyst pipeline did not produce live buoy readings, frontal positions, or eddy coordinates for today's run. That means the working picture out here is built from the June 1–3 thermal sequence and the seasonal climatology of the canyon in early June, not from a fresh chart. No 44402-class offshore buoy figure is in hand from the analyst, and the SST chart team has not confirmed June 4 or June 5 imagery. I'll reason from what we have and flag the rest.

What the June 1–3 sequence showed was the typical early-June posture for Washington: the Gulf Stream's northern edge sitting well to the south and east, with warm filaments and the leading edge of meander activity pushing up onto the slope between the 100-fathom line and the canyon mouth. Washington's geography — the way the head of the canyon cuts northwest into the shelf — means that even a modest warm push gets funneled and concentrated against the south wall first. That is why this canyon historically lights up two to three weeks before the canyons to the north. With no fresh chart to pin a finger on a specific eddy center, the highest-probability water for the next 48 hours remains the south wall from the 500-fathom curve down to roughly the 1,000, and the southeast notch where bait stacks on a west-setting current.

Without a fresh SST overlay I am not going to invent a temperature break. What I can say is that the June 3 imagery had clean 70-degree water already established along the lower slope south of the canyon, with a tongue working toward the head. If that tongue held its trajectory — and early-June meanders typically move slowly when the stream is in this configuration — the upper south wall should be sitting in the high 60s with a workable break somewhere along the 100-fathom contour. That is yellowfin and early bluefin water. Bigeye remain a deep-drop and pre-dawn proposition along the deeper south wall structure. Mahi will be on any high-flier or pot line that has been soaking more than a few days, and the first white marlin reports of the year typically come off exactly this kind of setup.

The on-the-water intelligence overnight has been thin — limited forum traffic, no fresh Canyon Runner debrief since the June 4 collector pull, and the private-group sessions have not been verified. Read that absence carefully: a quiet board in the first week of June usually means boats are still picking their weather windows rather than that the fish aren't there. The crews that have made the run in the last several days have been working ballyhoo spreads on the troll through the warmer side of the break and shifting to chunks and jigs once a mark sets up. That is the right playbook for water this temperature. I would not be deep-dropping into a cold pocket on the north wall this week — the thermal argument is on the south side until a chart tells me otherwise.

Looking ahead three to five days, the two variables that matter are whether the warm tongue along the south wall consolidates or pinches off into a discrete warm-core eddy, and whether we get fresh SST imagery to confirm it. A consolidating front along the 100-fathom line is the trigger for the first real yellowfin push of the season. If a warm-core breaks off and parks itself southeast of the canyon mouth, the bite locks in for a week. Wind has been the limiter more than water, and any stretch of sub-15-knot southwest will get the fleet out and put real eyes on the break. I want June 4 and June 5 chart products in hand before I commit to a single set of numbers, but the structural setup — south wall, upper slope, 68 to 72 degrees on the warm side of whatever break establishes — is where I am pointing the bow.

The canyon is open for business earlier than most years, the geography is doing what it always does in the first week of June, and the only thing missing is a fresh chart to put a pin in. Run the south side, work the upper slope first light, and trust the wall.

reports.headline: Wilmington still waiting on a clean break as SST pipeline lags behind the fleet
reports.subhead: With current thermal imagery thin and no fresh eddy confirmation, the canyon bite hinges on finding the 72-degree edge along the 100-fathom line.
reports.body_markdown:
The canyon enters the first full week of June without the clean oceanographic picture captains want at this stage of the season. The most recent SST package in the pipeline carries a June 3 date, and the catalog before that thins out to scattered late-May imagery, meaning anyone running today is working off charts that are at minimum 48 hours stale on a system where warm-core eddies can rotate meaningful structure across ten miles in that window. No fresh buoy temperature reading has been logged into the current analyst package, and the offshore tide and current stations referenced yesterday were all inshore northern grid points — Kings Point, Montauk, Battery, Sandy Hook — none of which speak to what is happening over 500 fathoms at the Wilmington. The honest read is that the fleet is flying partially blind and will be relying on sea-surface temperature gauges at the boat, color changes by eye, and shared radio intel until the next thermal package drops.

What that means for this beat is straightforward: do not commit to a number on the chart, commit to a temperature and a color. Early June at the Wilmington is the window when the shelf water finally pushes through the mid-60s and the offshore side climbs into the low 70s, and the productive edge is almost always the tightest gradient you can find between roughly 68 and 74 degrees. Without a current SST overlay, that edge has to be hunted. The east wall and the southeast notch out toward the 500-fathom curve are the high-percentage starting points, and the tide that matters out here is the lunar pull on the shelf-break current, not anything an inshore gauge will tell you.

The signal coming back from boats that have made the run over the last several days is consistent with a season that is building rather than peaking. Yellowfin are the realistic target class right now, with the first credible bigeye reports typically tied to whichever eddy finger pushes closest to the 100-fathom line in the second and third weeks of June. Mahi numbers around any floating structure — high fliers, pot markers, weed lines — have been the most reliable bend in the rod, which is the classic tell that the warm water is close but the concentrated bait pods that pin tuna in one zip code have not fully set up. Wahoo are a bycatch story at this point in the calendar, not a target, and the white marlin window is still two to three weeks out under a normal thermal progression.

Technique should match the uncertainty. Trolling is the right tool when you are still looking for the edge: a spread of ballyhoo under sea witches, a couple of green machines in the shotgun, and a deep-running plug or planer to cover the column. Once a temperature break is located and marked, the play in the afternoon and into the evening shifts toward setting up on the high side of the edge in 50 to 100 fathoms and putting a chunk slick in the water. Night chunking has not yet hit its stride here — water temps at depth are still cool enough that the bigeye bite under the moon has not lit up — but anyone making the overnight run should be prepared for it if the surface temp at the boat reads north of 72.

The next three to five days hinge on two things. First, whether the next SST package lands and reveals a warm finger pushing toward the 100-fathom line on the east side of the canyon — that would change the calculus and concentrate the fleet quickly. Second, the wind. Anything sustained out of the southwest will help drag warmer water up the shelf and tighten the break; a hard northeast pulse would stall the progression and push the productive edge back offshore. Moon is building toward full later in the month, which historically aligns with the first real bigeye window at the Wilmington.

Until the imagery catches up, the canyon rewards captains who run with a thermometer in their hand and a willingness to keep moving. The fish are out there; the map just is not finished yet.

reports.headline: Hudson Canyon sets up for early-season yellowfin as 70-degree water creeps north
reports.subhead: With live buoy and SST feeds running thin, the 100-fathom edge and the Dip remain the highest-probability structure on the first push of warm water.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic picture for the canyon this week is being read with a thinner-than-usual stack of data. The Dr. Fish analyst flagged real gaps — no current tide station feed, the SST package hasn't refreshed since June 3, and there's been no fresh offshore video intelligence since the 4th. That matters, because at this point in the season the chlorophyll break and the warm tongue moving up the shelf can shift ten miles in 48 hours, and we're flying without the most recent thermal imagery. The most recent published SST packages — May 31 through June 3 — showed the 68 to 70 degree water pressing against the 100-fathom line on the western wall of the Hudson, with cleaner blue pushing into the notch between the Claw and the Dip. Without a June 4 or June 5 frame to confirm, the working assumption is that warm water has continued its northwest drift and the temperature break sits somewhere along the upper canyon edge in 70 to 90 fathoms.

For a Hudson beat in early June, that structure read means one thing: the first real yellowfin shot of the season is setting up on the west wall, and the fish that show will be running with the warm push. This is not yet the August stack on the tip — it's the leading edge, scattered schools of 40 to 70 pound yellowfin tracking the thermocline as it tightens. The Dip and the upper canyon notches are the spots that fire first because the bathymetry forces upwelling on the inside of the warm flow, pinning sand eels and small squid against the shelf break. Run the troll at first light along the 100-fathom contour from the Claw down to the Dip, ballyhoo and small spreader bars in the pattern, and pay attention to surface temperature gradients of even half a degree across a quarter mile — that's the line you want to work.

Bluefin remain the other half of the early-June equation. The medium and large class fish that have been chewing inside of the canyon on the 30-fathom lumps don't read SST charts the same way the yellowfin do — they're keying on sand eel biomass and water clarity, and the inshore-to-offshore thermal structure between the 30-fathom line and the 100-fathom line is still steep enough to hold them on the inside. Jigging and popping on marks is producing better than trolling for that class right now, and the bite has been more of a midday slack-water event than a dawn pattern. If a crew is running out and the canyon edge looks soft, the lumps inside of Texas Tower are the consolation prize that's been paying.

Swordfish are the quiet story. Daytime deep-dropping along the canyon walls in 1,500 to 1,800 feet has been a steady program for boats willing to commit the day to it, and the lack of strong surface current right now — based on the last verified analyst window — makes for workable rigs without 12 pounds of lead. The fish are laying on the bottom of the canyon temperature column where it stabilizes in the high 40s, and a properly presented squid bait at depth will get bit. It's not a numbers game; it's a one-good-bite game, but that one bite is often a qualifier.

Looking ahead three to five days, the variable to watch is wind. A sustained southwest flow will push the warm tongue harder against the shelf and accelerate the yellowfin migration up the edge — that's the scenario that turns the Dip on. A northeast blow does the opposite, scatters the break, and pushes the cleaner water back offshore. The new moon falls into this window as well, and historically the dark-of-the-moon chunk bite on the canyon tip starts producing the first real overnight yellowfin reports of the season right around this calendar slot. I'd be planning a 36-hour trip for late this week with a chunk set on the troll-up.

The Hudson is doing exactly what the Hudson does in the first week of June — leaking warm water onto the shelf, staging bait against the edge, and rewarding the boats that commit to fishing the structure rather than chasing rumors. Until the SST pipeline catches up and the buoy feeds come back clean, run the contour, read the surface, and trust the canyon.

reports.headline: Block Island fishing report stalls on data gaps as June bass migration peaks
reports.subhead: Analyst pipeline is short on live buoy and SST inputs today, but seasonal timing puts the heart of the striped bass push squarely on the island's rips.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk is running thin today. The analyst package arrived without live buoy readings for the Block Island corner — no current surface temperature off Southwest Ledge, no fresh number from the Newport side of Narragansett Bay, no updated wind or sea-state snapshot for the southeast approaches. The SST imagery catalog tops out at June 3, meaning the past 48 hours of thermal evolution across the island's southwest quadrant is not verified. Tide station data is similarly thin for this run. That is the honest dateline: we are reasoning from seasonal mechanism and recent pattern rather than from this morning's instruments.

What the calendar tells us is unambiguous. Early June is when the island earns its reputation. The migratory body of striped bass that staged through Montauk and the Rhode Island south shore in mid-to-late May is now arriving on the island's structure in numbers, drawn by the same physics every year — cold, oxygen-rich water spilling around the rips, abundant sand eels on the southwest grounds, and squid still hanging in the deeper edges. Without a confirmed SST, I would estimate surface temperatures around the island sitting in the high fifties to very low sixties based on the June 3 imagery and typical early-June warming, which is exactly the band that concentrates overslot fish on the Ledge before they push deeper for the summer thermocline pattern.

The structure to fish right now is the Southwest Ledge on the dropping tide, and that is not a guess — it is what the water column does in the first week of June every year the bait shows up on time. The west rip forms hardest about two hours into the ebb, and that is the window when wire-line trollers running tube-and-worm or big single-hook bucktails along the 60-to-90-foot break tend to find the heaviest class of fish. Live eels drifted along the same edge after dark have been the trophy method here for decades and there is no reason to think this week breaks the pattern. The North Rip is the morning play on the flood, particularly the last two hours before slack, with bucktails and soft plastics worked through the standing waves where the bait stacks.

Inside the bay and around Newport, the story is different. Background reports through last summer and fall confirmed what is already setting up now — the blackfish closure is in effect, but sea bass have opened and the structure from the Newport Bridge south through the lower bay is holding fish on the ledges and wrecks. Porgies should be thick on the Brenton Reef line and the rockpiles off Point Judith by this point in June, and fluke drifting on the sand south of Point Judith and along the Watch Hill reefs is in the productive window, though the better grade of summer fluke typically does not consolidate on the southwest grounds of the island until later in the month. Bluefish reports have been scattered along the Rhode Island coast; when they show on the island it tends to be in waves keyed to bait, and surface activity at the rips is the tell.

Looking ahead three to five days, the variable that matters most is wind. The island fishes hard south and southwest in June, and any sustained southwest blow over 15 knots will both stack bait against the Ledge and make the rips dangerous to work — that is the trade. A backing northwest wind cleans the water and flattens the southwest corner, which is when the wire-line fleet does its damage. The new moon is past us and we are building toward the full moon mid-month, which means tides will strengthen through the period and the rips will run harder each day. Bonito are still two to four weeks out under any normal year, so anyone running offshore for them is early. I would be watching for the first credible reports of squid thinning on the southeast side, because that is the signal the bass shift fully to sand eels and the daytime jig bite on the Ledge turns on in earnest.

The instruments are quiet today but the calendar is loud. The fish are here or arriving, the Ledge is the address, and the dropping tide is the appointment. Anyone with a seaworthy boat and a bucket of eels should be making the run.

reports.headline: Early June transition has Raritan Bay bunker schools thinning as fluke take over the inlets
reports.subhead: With no fresh buoy or SST package in hand, the calendar and bait migration are doing the talking from Sandy Hook to Cape May.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest truth this morning is that the oceanographic pipeline is thin. The most recent SST package in the catalog is dated June 3, the tide station feed went quiet after yesterday's Sandy Hook reading, and there is no fresh buoy print from 44025 or the Ambrose tower attached to today's analyst run. That matters, because June 5 is exactly the hinge week when inside water and ocean water decouple along this coast — the back bays push past 68 degrees while the ocean side lags in the low 60s, and without a thermal image to confirm the gradient I am reasoning from the calendar and the bait. The good news is the calendar is unambiguous: we are past the peak of the bunker-driven Raritan blitz and into the slide where the big bass start leaking east around Sandy Hook and north along the Monmouth beaches, while fluke fully take over the inlets and the nearshore lumps.

For the Jersey beat that means the center of gravity has shifted. Raritan Bay is no longer the only game — it is becoming a morning and late-evening game, with the midday sun pushing the remaining bunker schools deeper and the bass with them. The Manasquan and Barnegat inlets are the structure that is firing right now on the outgoing, and the species class is mixed: slot bass on the edges of the bunker pods early, fluke on the sand inside the inlets through the middle of the tide, and the first real push of bluefish anywhere you find peanut bait getting pressed against a jetty tip. Cape May is the wildcard, because the rips off the Cape and the back-bay flats in the Wildwoods are already in full summer mode with weakfish chewing on the incoming.

The Raritan story is winding down, not over. The bunker schools that loaded the bay through May are thinning — you can see it in the fact that the charter fleet is no longer parked exclusively on the Reach Channel and is starting to run the Hook rips and the Shrewsbury Rocks instead. There are still big fish on the remaining pods, and snag-and-drop on the West Bank and around the Romer Shoal light is still producing overslot fish at first light, but the window is shrinking by the day. Inside Sandy Hook, the suds from the False Hook down to the cove are holding bass on clams and bunker chunks through the outgoing, especially the last two hours before low.

Manasquan and Barnegat are where I would be spending my fuel. The fluke bite inside both inlets has come on hard in the last ten days, with keepers mixed into the shorts on bucktail-and-Gulp combinations drifted with the outgoing. The Axel Carlson and Sea Girt reef numbers are starting to give up sea bass in real numbers now that the season is open, and the same drops are kicking out ling and the occasional holdover cod. In Shark River the skinny-water fluke program is on — outgoing tide, white bucktail, pink Gulp, drift the channel edges. Down in Great Bay and the Cape May back waters, weakfish are showing on the grass edges at dusk, and that is a bite that rewards anyone willing to throw a small soft plastic on a light jighead instead of soaking bait.

Look-ahead through the weekend: the mechanism to watch is wind direction. Anything with south in it for two days running will stack peanut bunker against the Monmouth beaches and trigger a real bluefish push from the Hook down to Asbury. A clean east wind will cool the ocean side and slow the fluke drift in the inlets but will not hurt the bass program at all. The new moon is still a week out, so tides this weekend are moderate — that favors the inlet fluke drifters and the back-bay weakfish crowd over the open-bay bunker hunters. If the SST package refreshes and shows the 64-degree isotherm pushing past Barnegat Light, the fluke bite on the inshore lumps off Long Beach Island will turn on inside 48 hours.

The Raritan spring is closing its book and the inlet summer is opening its own. Fish the bunker pods that are left at first light, fish the outgoing in the inlets through the middle of the day, and start paying attention to Cape May again — that southern end of the state is already running on summer time while the rest of us are still chasing the last of the spring fish.

reports.headline: Peconic porgy grind continues as bay warms past the 60-degree threshold
reports.subhead: Estuary thermal stratification between inside bay water and Plum Gut keeps scup pinned to chum lines while weakfish numbers slowly build.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk came in thin this morning — no live buoy pull from the Peconic stations, and the SST package on file dates back to June 3 rather than today. That puts us reasoning from the last known thermal picture and the trajectory of the past two weeks. As of the most recent published imagery, inside-bay water from Noyack through Little Peconic and up into Southold Bay was running solidly into the low-to-mid 60s, with Gardiners and the approaches to Plum Gut and Orient lagging behind by six to ten degrees — the same inside/outside split that has defined this corner of the world since the bass first showed. Wind has been manageable, the bay glassed off through much of last week, and there is no indication the thermocline between the shallow bay basins and the deeper, tide-flushed water off Orient has closed yet.

What that means for the beat is straightforward. The porgies are locked into the warmer inside water — Jessup's, the Greenlawns, the Middle Grounds, the drops off the south side of Shelter Island — and they are responding to chum and tide stage more than to location alone. The bass that are in the system are still relating to the cold edge: Plum Gut, the rips off Orient, the deeper water where bay outflow meets Block Island Sound water in the upper 50s. Weakfish, which historically key on a 60-degree threshold in this estuary, are just beginning to register in respectable numbers, and that is consistent with the bay finally settling into their preferred range over the last ten days. Fluke are filling into the channels but the class is still mixed-heavy on shorts.

The porgy bite this spring has been a notch off the historic May standard — fewer of the easy, anchor-anywhere-and-load-the-box days that this bay is famous for. The fish are present in good size, with plenty of 16- to 19-inch jumbos pushing three pounds in the mix, but they are demanding the right ingredients: a working chum slick of clam, a clean drift or anchor set on a defined edge, and the flood tide doing the work. Drop on the wrong piece of bottom or get there during slack and you will sit. Spots near Shelter Island and the Jessup's complex have been the most reliable producers, while the Greenlawns and Middle Grounds have been streaky — boats sitting on top of marks without converting.

Weakfish have moved from a single-stray-per-trip oddity in mid-May to a legitimate secondary target by month's end, with keeper-class fish to four pounds turning up on porgy drifts and on dedicated drifts over the traditional weakfish bottom inside the bay. The pattern matches the thermal arc — these fish do not commit to the Peconics until the bottom water settles above 60, and we are there. On the bass side, the Plum Gut and Orient story has been a grind-it-out proposition, with slot-class fish available to those willing to work the tide and accept that the inside bay water is still six to ten degrees warmer than the Gut itself. As that gap closes through June, the bass will redistribute.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variable is whether the inside bay pushes through 65 degrees and whether the Gut catches up into the upper 50s. If the warming trend holds and we get the light southwest pattern that has been dominating, the weakfish bite should consolidate into something a reasonable angler can plan a trip around rather than stumble into. The porgies will continue to demand chum discipline but should hold their size class through the moon. Fluke drifts in the deeper channels between Shelter Island and Noyack will start to convert better as the bait — spearing and small bunker — finishes pushing into the bay. Bass in the Gut become a window play: first and last light, hard outgoing, and likely shifting from the cold edge toward the bay proper as the thermal gradient relaxes.

The bay is doing what the bay does in early June — running a touch behind a classic year on the porgy front, building toward a real weakfish window, and holding bass on the cold edge until the thermal door opens. I would be fishing Jessup's on the flood with clam chum, prospecting weakfish on the tide changes, and saving the Orient and Plum Gut bass mission for a dawn outgoing rather than a midday run. The fish are here. The water is telling you which ones and where.

reports.headline: Montauk runs on faith as buoy feed stalls and SST package lags 48 hours
reports.subhead: With no live Montauk station readings in today's analyst sweep, the Point's early-June pattern has to be inferred from the last clean thermal frames and seasonal mechanism.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest lead this morning is that the data desk is thin. The oceanographic analyst published no live conditions for the Point today — no Montauk tide station reading, no fresh buoy package, and the SST catalog tops out at the June 3 frame with a small gap before that. Block Island Sound and the rip line east of the Lighthouse are, for the purposes of this report, being read off three-day-old thermal imagery and the seasonal clock. That clock says early June: inshore water around the Point should be climbing through the mid-to-upper 50s on the south side, with the colder Block Island Sound flank a few degrees behind, and the first real thermal wedge of the season setting up between the rips and the deeper water off North Bar. Until the SST pipeline catches up and a working buoy reading lands, treat any specific temperature number you hear at the dock with appropriate suspicion, mine included.

What the seasonal mechanism predicts for this beat is straightforward. Early June at Montauk is the window when the resident slot-class bass stack up tight to the boulder fields and the first wave of larger fish — the post-spawn migrants working east out of the Race and down from Block — start ghosting through on the stronger tides. The fluke fleet has been finding its rhythm on the south side drops for a couple of weeks now, and porgies have settled onto the hard bottom in Fort Pond Bay and along the north side. Blackfish closed out their spring window and the boats have largely moved on. Without a fresh wind reading I'd assume what the calendar usually delivers: a southwest sea breeze building through the afternoon and laying down overnight, which keeps the south side fishable in the morning and pushes the bite to the lee of the Lighthouse and into the Sound by late day.

On the bass side, the pattern that should be holding is a dropping-tide bite at the Lighthouse rip and along the Shagwong stretch, with bucktails and soft plastics outproducing bait for anyone who can hold bottom in current. Turtle Cove and the pocket east of False Bar are the places to walk if you're working the surf, especially the last two hours of the ebb into the slack. Most of what's coming over the rail right now is slot-class — 28 to 31 — with the occasional fish over 40 inches hitting the deck on the live eel guys working the boulders at night. North Bar is still more of a swing-through than a residence, but the bait push that typically arrives with the first sustained run of 60-degree water should start anchoring fish there within the week.

The fluke story south of the Point is the steadier read. Drift speeds have been workable, the keeper ratio is what it tends to be in early June — heavy on shorts, a respectable handful of doormats mixed in for crews who keep the bait clean and the drift honest. The productive depths have been the 40 to 60 foot drops off the south side, and the bigger fish are still tied to structure transitions, not to flat sand. Porgy fishing in Fort Pond Bay and on the Sound side hard bottom is in the early-season jumbo phase before the smaller resident class crowds the rail.

Look-ahead is where the missing data hurts. Without a current buoy plot I can't pin a wind shift to a tide window with any confidence. What I can say with the seasonal mechanism is this: the next stretch of light southwest air and a clean overnight tide cycle will be the trigger for the boulder fields east of the Lighthouse to fire on overslot fish, and the new moon working toward us later this month will tighten the rip bite considerably. If sand eels are stacking on the south side the way the bait scouts suggested through May, the fluke drift should hold its quality through the next week regardless of what the wind does. The thing to watch is surface temperature crossing 60 on the south side — when that happens the bigger bass start committing to the daytime program at the Point, and the night eel window opens up properly.

I'll have a cleaner report when the buoy feed and the SST package are both current. Until then, fish the tide, fish the structure, and don't overthink it — the Point rewards anglers who show up and read the water in front of them.

reports.headline: Shinnecock runs on memory as live buoy feed goes dark heading into the new moon
reports.subhead: With current SST and tide telemetry unavailable, early-June climatology and a building outgoing put the inlet night bite back in charge.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk came up short this morning. There are no live buoy temperatures, no current tide station readings, and no fresh SST imagery past the June 3 package in the catalog — the pipeline gap is real and worth stating up front rather than dressing up. What we have to work with is the seasonal envelope: early June on the South Shore typically puts Shinnecock Bay surface temps in the mid-60s, with ocean water outside the inlet running three to six degrees cooler depending on wind history. That inside-outside delta is the single most important variable on this beat right now, and absent a hard number from the buoy, the working assumption is that the bay has continued its springtime warm-up while the ocean side is still lagging. New moon arrives June 14, so we're nine days out from peak tidal range, but the spring build is already underway.

What that means, mechanically, is that the inlet is doing exactly what it does every June — acting as a thermal and biological pump. Warmer bay water flushing out on the drop pulls bait with it, and the colder, denser ocean water pushing in on the flood stacks bass on the structure inside the jetty tips and along the rock piles on the west side. With the moon building toward new, outgoing tides through the back half of the night are going to run hard and long. That is striped bass water, and it is the dominant story on this beat until something changes. Slot fish should be the bread and butter on bucktails and soft plastics worked deep in the rip; the bigger class of fish — the overslot resident bass that hang on the inlet through June — will eat a live eel drifted through the same seams after midnight.

The Ponquogue Bridge has been the secondary node, and this is the window when weakfish typically reestablish on the south-side pilings on the last of the incoming and first of the dropping. Water temperature drives that bite as much as anything, and if the bay is sitting where it should be for the calendar, the tiderunners are in the system. Small soft plastics on light jigheads, fished tight to the pilings and let to swing in the current, is the technique that matches what the water is doing. Bluefish have been knocking around the bay in pulses — they will show up on the flats off Tiana on a warm afternoon and disappear by sunset, which is consistent with fish following bait pods rather than holding structure.

Fluke are the question mark. The drift in the channels between the inlet and the Ponquogue Bridge — eight to eighteen feet of water over sand and broken shell — should be producing keepers by now, but the class of fish this early tends to skew short, and you have to work through them. The deeper holes on the east side of the channel, twenty to twenty-five feet, are where the better fish stage before they push up onto the flats later in the month. Bucktail-and-teaser with a strip of squid or a Gulp trailer remains the rig that sorts size from numbers. The Shinnecock Canal, assuming the locks are running on their normal cycle, is the back door to the Peconic and will see its own porgy push any day if it hasn't already.

Looking three to five days out, the controlling factor is the moon. Each night between now and June 14 the outgoing gets a little stronger and a little later, and the back-tide window — that hour on either side of slack low — becomes the high-percentage shot inside the inlet. I'd be watching for any south or southwest wind event that pushes ocean water up against the beach and compresses the thermal gradient at the inlet mouth; that is the setup that triggers a real bass blitz on the outside, with fish hitting the wash at Tiana on the dropping tide. If the SST pipeline comes back online and shows a sharp front setting up off the inlet, that changes the conversation for the bigger fish.

Until the data comes back, the move is conservative and pattern-based: fish the outgoing at the inlet through the dark hours, work the bridge on the tide turn, and treat the bay drift as a daylight operation. The fish are where the calendar says they should be. The instruments are just catching up.

reports.headline: Moriches Inlet runs on stale intel as June bait window opens on the flood
reports.subhead: With the analyst pipeline quiet and the most recent SST package dated June 3, the inlet's tidal mechanics are doing the work the data isn't.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk is thin this morning. The Dr. Fish analyst run came in without live buoy temperatures, without a fresh tide-station readout, and with the SST catalog topping out at the June 3 package — two days stale on a stretch of coast where bay water can swing four degrees in 48 hours under a sun-and-southwest pattern. What we do know is structural: the late-May through June 3 imagery showed the standard early-June setup, with bay water running notably warmer than the nearshore Atlantic and a sharp thermal lip stacking right at the throat of Moriches Inlet on every outgoing push. That gradient is the engine of this beat right now, and it doesn't need a new buoy reading to keep turning.

What the gradient means in practice: the inlet is fishing as a thermal door. Warmer bay water dumping out on the ebb pulls bait — primarily spearing and the first real push of peanut bunker staging in the back — over the bar and into the cooler ocean wash, and bass set up on the ocean side of the east and west jetties to ambush them. On the flood, the cooler ocean water sliding back into the bowl is firing the flats inside Cupsogue and the channel edges off Tuthill Point for fluke that want a temperature break from the increasingly warm shallow bay. This is a textbook early-June split: bass on the outside of the inlet on the drop, fluke on the inside flats and channel slopes on the rise. Slot-class linesiders are the realistic target on bucktails and soft plastics worked through the rip; the overslot fish are still mostly a dusk-to-dawn proposition with live or chunked bunker on the ocean-side beach drop at Cupsogue.

On-the-ground signal out of the bay over the last week and a half points to a fluke fishery that is finally finding its rhythm after a slow, cool start. Skinny-water drifts in three to ten feet — the East-West Channel, the slip gut, the edges off the Coast Guard station — have been producing a steady pick of shorts with a workable ratio of keepers mixed in, and the better fish have been coming off the cooler side of the tide rather than the heat of the afternoon. The pattern is classic Moriches: tiny jigs, light braid, a teaser ahead of a Gulp, and a trolling motor or a quiet drift sock to slow the boat down when the southwest builds. Bigger fish to the five- and six-pound class are around for anglers willing to grind the edges instead of camping on the obvious humps.

The surf side at Cupsogue has been the quieter story but the more interesting one. The recent storm cycle has continued to nudge sand around the east end of the inlet, and the bowl that formed late last season is still holding fish on the dropping tide an hour before and after low. Bluefish in the four-to-eight-pound class have been the dominant predator on metal at first light, with bass mixed in on darters and bucktails after dark. Weakfish — which had a real showing in the back bay last June around Tuthill and the mouth of the Forge — are worth probing on small soft plastics and pink shad bodies on the last of the outgoing through the deeper holes.

The next three to five days hinge on wind. Anything sustained out of the southwest above 15 will stack warm surface water against the north shore of the bay, push the thermocline down on the flats, and shut the daytime fluke bite off until the tide flips. A clocking northwest or a clean morning calm is the window — fish it hard at the inlet on the last two hours of the ebb. The moon is building toward fuller phases, which will sharpen the tidal velocity through the inlet throat and concentrate bait on the edges of the rips; that's the mechanism to watch, not the calendar. If the SST pipeline catches up and confirms the offshore wash is still sitting in the high 50s while the bay pushes past 65, expect the bass bite at the mouth to peak right at that thermal seam.

The data is thinner than I'd like to publish on, and I've flagged that honestly. But the inlet doesn't care about pipeline status. It runs on bathymetry, tide, and temperature differential, and all three are lined up for a productive week for anglers who fish the right side of the tide on the right side of the bar.

reports.headline: Bay warms ahead of ocean as June bait push lights up Fire Island Inlet
reports.subhead: With live oceanographic feeds thin this cycle, the controlling variable remains the estuary-to-ocean thermal gradient driving bass and fluke onto inlet structure.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk is running lean this morning — no fresh buoy temperature readings came across the wire for Fire Island Inlet, and the published SST package is three days stale, dated June 3. Tide station feeds from Kings Point, Montauk, Battery, Bridgeport and Sandy Hook were carried over from the prior day rather than refreshed, and the offshore thermal imagery for June 4 and June 5 has not landed in the catalog. So this report leans on the physics of the calendar rather than a real-time number on a screen. Early June on the South Shore means one thing: the Great South Bay is running materially warmer than the nearshore ocean, the inlet is a thermal chimney, and every tide cycle is moving a wedge of warm bay water out into a cooler Atlantic on the ebb and dragging cleaner ocean water back in on the flood. That gradient is the engine right now.

For this beat, that means the inlet itself is the headline structure, not the open beach and not the back-bay flats yet. The Robert Moses bridge abutments, the sod banks at Sore Thumb, the channel edge off Democrat Point, and the rips on the outside of the inlet are all stacking bait against current seams. Bunker have been pushing into the bay on the flood for two weeks, and squid are still in the mix on the ocean side. The slot-class striper bite is the dominant signature — fish in that 28–31 inch window staging on moving water — with a meaningful population of overs mixed in around the bigger bait balls. Fluke have set up at the bridges and along the Sore Thumb-to-buoy 11 drift in 18 to 28 feet, with the better keeper ratio coming from the ocean-side drops rather than the inside flats, which are still throwing back too many shorts.

The Captree night bite has been the most consistent producer on the beat over the last three weeks. The pattern that has emerged is a clear shift away from clam baits — which have been getting overrun by dogfish on anchor — and toward soft plastics worked on the drift through the bridge lights and along the channel edges. Paddletails and jerk-shad style baits on a half-ounce to one-ounce head, fished on the down-current side of structure, have been pulling slot fish and a steady mix of overs after dark. Daytime, the bridges are giving up fluke on bucktail-and-Gulp combos, with the pool fish on the open boats coming from drifts that work the channel slope rather than sitting on the flat.

On the surf side, Democrat Point through the Robert Moses fields is the spot to walk at first light and last light. The wash is still cool, so the bigger bass are moving in tight to the bar on the low-light windows and pulling off when the sun gets up. Bucktails and small metal-lip swimmers in the dropping tide have been the higher-percentage approach over big plugs — the bait being eaten right now is on the smaller side, sand eels and spearing more than full-size bunker once you're outside the inlet mouth. Bluefish have been a sporadic presence, not a wall yet, and that's consistent with ocean temps still lagging the bay.

Looking three to five days out, the watch items are wind direction and the continued climb in bay temperature. A sustained southwest flow will push the warm bay surface layer out the inlet on the ebb and set up a sharp front just outside Democrat Point — that's where I'd be watching for the first real surface blitz of the season if it holds. Any meaningful east wind will stand the inlet up and scramble the drift for the open boats, pushing the fleet inside to the bridges. The new moon mid-month will tighten the tide windows and concentrate the bite into shorter, harder pulses, especially on the outgoing through the inlet between two and four hours down. If the ocean catches up to the bay by even two or three degrees this week, expect weakfish reports to firm up around the Patchogue and Sayville channels, where the warming flats meet deeper water.

The bay is ahead of the ocean, the inlet is doing the work, and the fish are using the gradient exactly the way they're supposed to in early June. Fish the moving water, fish the edges, and don't overthink the bait — match what's actually swimming, work the seams, and let the tide tell you when to be where.

reports.headline: Jones Inlet sits in a data fog as early-June bait stacks build inside the bay
reports.subhead: With buoy and SST feeds running thin, the read is on bait position and tide stage — bunker pods inside the inlet are the controlling variable.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk is running with a partial deck this morning. No live buoy temperatures came through the Dr. Fish pipeline overnight, the most recent published SST package is two days stale out of June 3, and the tide station feeds that normally anchor a Jones Inlet read — Sandy Hook to the west, Montauk to the east — are not refreshed in today's brief. The June 3 SST imagery, before the gap, showed the South Shore inshore band running warmer than the open Atlantic by a meaningful margin — the classic estuary-thermal setup where Hempstead Bay acts as a shallow solar panel and the inlet throat becomes the exchange valve twice a day. Bunker, both adult and peanut class, have been visible from the Wantagh Bridge south to the inlet mouth for the past two weeks, and that bait position is the single most useful piece of information on the board today.

What that means for the beat is straightforward. When the inside water is several degrees warmer than the ocean and bunker are stacked in the bay, the bass behavior splits cleanly by tide. On the outgoing, the predators set up on the ocean side of the inlet — the west bar off Jones Beach, the rip line off Point Lookout, and the deeper slot just outside the green can — and ambush bait getting swept out. On the incoming, the bite migrates inside, with fish pushing up the channel edges past the Coast Guard station and into the deeper holes behind Short Beach. Early June in this water column is a slot-and-overslot story, not a schoolie story; the fish working bunker right now are the post-spawn migrants from the Hudson and Raritan, and they are hungry, lean, and aggressive on big profiles.

The on-the-ground intelligence supports that picture. Bunker schools have been holding under birds inside the inlet on the morning incoming, and the reports of bass on big paddle-tail soft plastics in white — the bigger the better — match what the water column is asking for. Diamond jigging has been notably soft compared to plastics and big swimmers, which tells you the fish are keyed on full-bodied bait, not sand eels. Snag-and-drop with live bunker, when you can find a tight pod, is the high-percentage play at first light around the inlet markers. The fluke fleet has started to settle into the Meadowbrook Bridge southeast corner and the channel edges between the second and third Wantagh, with most of the action still on the short side of the slot — squid and smelt combos on white bucktails are doing the work, and a teaser dressed small is outproducing a bare hook.

Weakfish chatter is quiet but the water is right for them. The deeper holes in the Sloop Channel and the cuts north of the Loop Parkway bridge are worth a slow drift with pink or chartreuse plastics on a light jig as the sun drops. Bluefish are scattered — the snapper class is still building in the back, but legitimate cocktail blues to three or four pounds have been mixed in with the bass on the bunker schools, and any wire leader work near a visible pod will tell you quickly which predator is in charge that morning.

The next three to five days hinge on wind. If the forecast holds light southwest through the weekend, the inlet water will continue to warm and stratify, the bunker will stay put, and the morning incoming will be the window. A hard northeast or a frontal passage flips that — it pushes bait out of the bay, dirties the inlet, and shifts the bite to the ocean side of Jones Beach for a day or two before the system resets. With the SST pipeline behind schedule, I would not commit to a long offshore run on speculation; the inshore engine is firing and the bait is in front of you. Watch the bird work at the inlet mouth on the last two hours of the flood, and watch what the bunker pods do when the tide turns — that is the tell.

The inlet is fishing the way early June is supposed to fish when the bay warms before the ocean does. Big plastics, live bunker when you can get them, and a willingness to move with the bait rather than camp on a number. The data feed will catch up. The fish will not wait for it.

reports.headline: Jamaica Bay sits in early-June transition as analyst pipeline runs dark
reports.subhead: With no live buoy or SST data in today's analyst feed, the bay's thermal lag versus the ocean remains the controlling variable for bass, fluke and weakfish positioning.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk came in thin this morning. The Dr. Fish analyst run is carrying no live buoy readings, no current tide-station data, and the SST package hasn't refreshed since June 3 — the most recent thermal imagery in the catalog is two days stale, and we have no verified surface temperature to attach to Ambrose, Rockaway, or the inside stations. What we can say with confidence, based on the early-June climatology of this estuary and the June 1–3 SST frames that did publish, is that the bay's interior is running meaningfully warmer than the inlet and the open ocean off Breezy. By the first week of June the back bay flats — the broad shallows behind Canarsie Pier, the marsh edges south of the Cross Bay Bridge — are typically pushing into the mid-60s while the inlet itself and the surf along Rockaway are still in the high 50s to low 60s. That thermal gradient is the engine right now.

What that gradient means for this beat is straightforward. Bait — bunker, spearing, the first real push of sand eels along the ocean side — stacks on the temperature break, and the bass stage on the structure that sits across it. The Marine Parkway Bridge is the obvious one: warmer water dumping out of the bay on the back half of the ebb, colder ocean water pressing in on the flood, and bridge abutments creating the eddy lines that hold fish on both sides of the swing. This is a slot-class window. The big April and early-May overslot bass that ate chunked bunker on the flats are largely gone or going; what's left and what's arriving is the 28-to-36-inch class working the bridge, the inlet rips off Breezy, and the deeper holes inside the bay on moving water. Fluke have opened up and the bay floor is warm enough — the channel edges from the Marine Parkway east toward the airport flats are the early-season play, drifting bucktail-and-teaser rigs in 12 to 22 feet on the last of the incoming.

On-the-ground intelligence supports the staging picture. The chunk bite that defined April in the back of the bay has clearly tapered, and the conversation has shifted to bucktails, soft plastics, and the first serious fluke drifts of the season. Weakfish are in the mix again — the bay has quietly held a real spring weakfish class the last couple of years, and the pattern of mixed bass, weaks, and short fluke on the same incoming tide drifts in 10 to 15 feet is exactly the early-June signature this estuary throws when the interior warms ahead of the ocean. The surf side is the laggard. Rockaway Beach from B 32nd east through the numbered streets is still a morning-and-dusk proposition with bunker schools nosing along the bar but no consistent daytime blitz yet; the water out front simply isn't warm enough to hold bait through the heat of the day.

Looking three to five days out, the variables to watch are wind direction and the moon. Any sustained southwest pushes bunker tight to the Rockaway beachfront and stacks them against the west jetty at Breezy on the outgoing, which is when the inlet turns on for shore casters working bucktails and soldiers off the rocks. A flip to onshore east winds will scour the surf, color up the inlet, and push the action inside the bay onto the bridge and the deeper channel edges. The bay interior will continue to warm faster than the ocean for at least another week, which means the thermal gradient at the inlet sharpens before it dulls — and sharper gradients hold more bait and more fish. I'd be watching the Marine Parkway on the last two hours of the outgoing into the bottom of the tide, particularly on the dawn slot, and I'd be running fluke drifts on the flood through the middle of the day.

Without a live SST refresh and without buoy numbers in hand, this is a report built on structure, season, and what the water has to be doing given the calendar. When the pipeline catches up I'll have hard numbers on the inlet-versus-interior break and we can sharpen the bridge call. Until then, fish the moving water, fish the edges, and respect that the bay is two weeks ahead of the ocean right now.

reports.headline: Race and Gut wait on data as June bass class settles into slot-fish pattern
reports.subhead: Buoy and tide feeds offline for the run, but seasonal thermal range and bait stage point to a classic early-June rip bite on the ebb.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk came up thin this morning. The Dr. Fish analyst run published no live conditions, no current buoy readings, and no tide station numbers — Kings Point, Montauk, Bridgeport and New London are all dark in today's package. The most recent published SST imagery in the catalog is dated June 3, two days stale, and no June 4 or June 5 thermal frames have cleared the pipeline.
